```{r setup}
library(prepR4pcm)
```

## What “Latin-aware” means here

Botanical species names can differ because an adjectival epithet changes its
ending to agree with the gender of a genus. For example, the Code gives
*Bromus mollis* and *Geranium molle* as adjectival forms in different genera.
That pattern can help a matcher find a candidate. It does not prove that the
two names refer to the same taxon.

prepR4pcm's Latin-aware fuzzy matching is deliberately narrow. It reuses
`pr_suggest_gender()` to identify pairs in two common ending groups:
`-us/-a/-um` and `-is/-e`. Those pairs receive an ending-aware spelling score,
but the matcher allows them through only when the supplied taxonomic evidence
has the same accepted identifier, provider, snapshot, and rank. If that
evidence is absent, ambiguous, or conflicting, the pair remains available for
review and is not returned as an automatic fuzzy match.

The helper can show the possible endings in a reference list:

```{r ending-suggestions}
pr_suggest_gender("Plant albus", c("Plant alba", "Plant album"))
```

These constructed names demonstrate string handling; they are not claims about
published taxa. `pr_suggest_gender()` keeps every matching alternative and
marks every row as requiring review. It does not alter a reconciliation.

## Genus guides candidate search

Fuzzy candidate generation starts with names whose genus spellings are close.
This follows Erick Lundgren's suggestion to work with genus evidence before
species epithets. A strict genus cutoff would miss names transferred between
genera, so a broader fallback is available when the same comparable authority
identifies both spellings with the same accepted ID. The name score still
reports spelling similarity; authority identity is kept separate from that
score. A tree's branch placement is not used as independent identity evidence.

## The grammatical limit

The International Code of Nomenclature says adjectival specific epithets
agree with the generic name's gender. Nouns in apposition, genitive nouns,
nouns with accompanying adjectives in the genitive, and adverbs keep their
own endings. The Code also recognizes epithets whose
grammatical category is ambiguous; resolving that ambiguity can depend on a
published nomenclatural choice. These distinctions mean that a string ending
alone cannot tell software whether an epithet is an adjective or whether it
should change. This package does not parse Latin, infer adjective classes, or
determine genus gender.

The ending groups implemented here are candidate patterns, not a complete
account of botanical Latin. Greek-derived forms, other Latin declensions,
irregular forms, historical orthography, and ambiguous published usages are
outside this helper's coverage. The rules above are grounded in the current
[Madrid Code online](https://www.iaptglobal.org/madrid-code-online), especially
Articles 23.1, 23.5, and 23.6.

## What to do with a review candidate

Unresolved names can still have useful suggestions. The ordinary review command
`reconcile_review(result, type = "flagged")` includes pending candidate pairs
as well as flagged matches. `reconcile_summary(result)` reports these pairs;
`reconcile_summary(result, format = "data.frame")$tables$review_candidates`
returns the pending review table. Inspect the full evidence record with
`reconcile_candidates(result)`. The dedicated
`reconcile_review(result, type = "identity_candidates")` mode remains available.

Some suggested tree names may already be assigned to another input name. These
pairs remain visible with a warning. Review the competing names and resolve the
existing assignment before accepting the new pair. A suggestion never reserves
a tree tip or changes the mapping. `include_flagged = TRUE` applies existing
flagged mappings; it does not accept pending candidate pairs. Accepting a pair
during review records a deliberate override.

If the authority does not establish a matching identity, check an appropriate
taxonomic source yourself. Record a deliberate decision with
`reconcile_override()` or `reconcile_override_batch()`; do not treat a
grammatical-looking ending as a taxonomic crosswalk.

For the related spelling-only review helper, see the “Reviewing grammatical
endings” section in the [getting-started article](getting-started.html).
